question: What is the simple definition of poisoning in a clinical setting?

options.A: A chronic vitamin deficiency caused by poor dietary intake
options.B: Any substance that interferes with normal body functions after entering the body
options.C: An infection resulting from bacterial contamination in food
options.D: An allergic reaction to a newly prescribed antibiotic medication

explanation: You've got this! Think of poisoning simply as anything—a chemical, a drug, or a toxin—that disrupts how the body normally works once it gets inside. Great job! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h1)

question: How do accidental and intentional poisonings usually look different when patients arrive?

options.A: Accidental cases frequently involve children and single agents, while intentional cases often involve adults and multiple drugs
options.B: Intentional poisonings are completely untreatable compared to accidental exposures
options.C: Intentional poisonings only occur through inhalation, whereas accidental poisonings always involve swallowing
options.D: Accidental exposures never require medical attention, unlike all intentional exposures

explanation: Spot on! Little ones often accidentally swallow just one household item, whereas intentional adult cases more often involve multiple medications. Knowing this helps you prepare for what to expect! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h1)

question: What is the most common way people get poisoned right inside their own homes?
explanation: Well done! Swallowing things—like accidental medications or household cleaners—is by far the top way poisoning happens at home. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h2)

question: Why do toxins breathed into the lungs (inhalation) affect the body so quickly?

options.A: The stomach acid breaks down inhaled gases faster than swallowed solids
options.B: Skin pores open wider when toxic fumes are breathed into the room
options.C: Inhaled toxins must first pass through the liver before reaching the brain
options.D: Gases pass directly from the lung alveoli into the rich capillary blood supply

explanation: Think about the tiny air sacs (alveoli) in our lungs—they have a massive blood supply, letting gases jump straight into the bloodstream almost instantly! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h2)

question: What is your very first priority when a poisoned patient arrives in the emergency unit?

options.A: Asking family members about the patient's financial history
options.B: Stabilizing vital functions using the ABCDE approach
options.D: Inducing vomiting to empty the stomach contents

explanation: Safety first! Always check Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABCDE) before trying to figure out exactly what poison was swallowed. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h3)

question: A patient is rushed in unconscious, with very tiny pupils (pinpoint) and slow, shallow breathing. What type of poison do you suspect?
explanation: You nailed it! Pinpoint pupils combined with depressed breathing are the classic textbook signs of an opioid overdose. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h3)

question: Why is it a big mistake to make someone vomit after they swallow a corrosive chemical (like strong acid)?

options.A: It always causes permanent paralysis of the vocal cords
options.B: It forces the poison directly into the urinary bladder
options.C: It neutralizes all antidote medications given later in the hospital
options.D: It can cause additional severe burns to the esophagus as the chemical comes back up

explanation: Brilliant thinking! Corrosive chemicals burn on the way down, and forcing them back up means they burn the throat a second time. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h4)

question: What should you do immediately if a patient gets a chemical splashed into both eyes?

options.A: Flush the eyes continuously with clean water or normal saline for at least fifteen minutes
options.B: Rub the eyes firmly with a dry towel to remove solid particles
options.C: Put neutral cooking oil directly into the eyes to coat the chemical
options.D: Apply tight gauze patches over both eyes and wait for an ophthalmologist

explanation: Water is your best friend here! Long, continuous flushing washes away caustic chemicals before they can damage the cornea. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h4)

question: How does activated charcoal help treat someone who swallowed a poison?

options.A: It dilates blood vessels to speed up renal excretion
options.B: It coats the lungs to block toxic gas inhalation
options.C: It binds to toxins in the gut to prevent their absorption into the bloodstream
options.D: It neutralizes stomach acid to prevent chemical ulcers

explanation: Activated charcoal acts like a microscopic sponge, holding onto the toxins in the stomach and gut so they don't enter the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h5)

question: Why is stomach pumping (gastric lavage) rarely done if a patient seeks help hours after swallowing a poison?

options.A: Gastric lavage only works on poisons that were inhaled
options.B: The poison has already passed from the stomach into the small intestines
options.C: Activated charcoal neutralizes the need for any washing
options.D: The stomach lining becomes too tough for tubes to pass safely

explanation: Makes total sense, right? If hours have passed, the poison has already moved past the stomach, making pumping ineffective. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h5)

question: Which specific medication is the go-to emergency antidote for an opioid overdose?
explanation: Fantastic! Naloxone quickly blocks opioids and helps the patient breathe normally again. Keep this one locked in your memory! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h6)

question: A patient recovering from an intentional overdose is now awake and stable. What nursing action is most important?

options.A: Restricting all family visits to punish the patient for the suicide attempt
options.B: Providing continuous observation and psychological support while keeping the environment safe
options.C: Avoiding any conversation about the incident to prevent embarrassment
options.D: Discharging the patient immediately with a prescription for sedatives

explanation: You've got this. Emotional support and a safe, watch-careful environment are vital for anyone recovering from self-harm. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h6)

question: What is a common long-term problem for a patient who survives swallowing a corrosive chemical?

options.A: Chronic swelling of the lower limbs
options.C: Permanent hearing loss in both ears

explanation: When caustic burns heal, they form scar tissue. In the esophagus, this scarring narrows the tube, making swallowing difficult later on. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h7)

question: How can community nurses best help parents prevent accidental poisoning in toddlers?

options.A: Advising families to transfer all cleaning chemicals into empty soda bottles
options.B: Recommending that households avoid buying any chemical products entirely
options.C: Encouraging parents to induce vomiting in children at the first sign of illness
options.D: Teaching parents to store medications and cleaning agents in locked cabinets out of reach

explanation: Prevention is key! Keeping dangerous items locked away out of a toddler's curious reach is the best way to keep them safe. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h7)
